callouts.label: Equity
callouts.hint: Find the violet petal on the far left where a wheelchair user, a parent with a stroller, an older adult with a cane, and a student with a backpack share one sunny bench and table.
callouts.description: Equity asks a building to support a just and equitable world (ILFI). It should be open to people of all abilities and incomes and fair to the neighborhood around it. This is the society leg of the triple bottom line in Chapter 19: a building that only some people can reach or afford has not given much back.

callouts.label: Beauty
callouts.hint: Find the teal petal in the upper left with a curved sculptural stair rail and a colorful painted wall in swirling shapes.
callouts.description: Beauty celebrates design that uplifts the human spirit (ILFI). Sculpture, craft, and art are treated as part of performance, not decoration added at the end. Brand's How Buildings Learn argues that buildings people love tend to be maintained and kept, which ties beauty to durability (Chapter 21).
callouts.tip: A building nobody loves is the first one that gets torn down.

callouts.label: Place
callouts.hint: Find the green petal at the top with a tree-lined footpath, native prairie grass, a pond edge, and a few walkers and a cyclist.
callouts.description: Place asks a project to restore a healthy relationship with nature, not merely avoid harming the land it sits on (ILFI). The picture is a walkable, restored site with native plantings. Site analysis in Chapter 9 is where a design team learns what the land, soil, and groundwater already offer.

callouts.label: Living Building
callouts.hint: Find the small modern building in the middle of the flower with solar panels on its roof, glowing orange windows, and all seven petals reaching toward it.
callouts.description: ILFI describes a Living Building as regenerative: it connects occupants to light, air, food, nature, and community. The Challenge has 20 imperatives across the seven petals, ten core and ten that push performance further, and certification rests on measured performance after 12 months of occupancy, not on predictions.
callouts.tip: The seven petals are one flower. A project cannot skip the petals it finds inconvenient.

callouts.label: Water
callouts.hint: Find the blue petal in the upper right with a tall rain barrel on a stand, a downspout feeding it, and a roof planted with low green sedum.
callouts.description: Water asks a development to stay within the water balance of its location and climate (ILFI). Rain is treated as a resource: collected in a cistern, slowed by a green roof, and used or returned on site. Chapter 19 covers efficient fixtures and collected rainwater, and Chapter 13 covers green roofs.

callouts.label: Less Bad Building
callouts.hint: Find the gray building in the lower-left panel with thick dark arrows carrying resources in and an even larger gray cloud and waste stream going out.
callouts.description: Less-bad thinking measures success by how much harm is reduced compared with a typical building. The building still takes in energy, water, and materials from outside and sends waste and emissions out. That is real progress, but the flow arrows still point mostly one way: it takes more than it gives.

callouts.label: Materials
callouts.hint: Find the brown petal in the lower left with a wooden beam stack, a clear glass jar of ingredients, and a clipboard with rows of checked boxes.
callouts.description: Materials asks for products that remain safe for all species over time (ILFI). The clipboard stands for knowing what a product contains and where it came from. Chapter 20 gives the tools: Health Product Declarations, environmental product declarations, low-VOC products, embodied carbon, and local sourcing.

callouts.label: Health and Happiness
callouts.hint: Find the rose-pink petal in the lower right with a bright room, a tall window casting a sunbeam on the floor, an open window, and a potted plant by a desk.
callouts.description: Health and Happiness asks for environments that enhance physical and psychological well-being (ILFI). Daylight, fresh air, and a view of nature are the picture's clues. Chapter 19 covers daylighting, Chapter 4 covers ventilation and thermal comfort, and Chapter 20 covers the low-emitting products that keep indoor air clean.

callouts.label: Energy
callouts.hint: Find the golden petal on the right with a tilted field of dark-blue solar panels and a small wind vane under a bright sun.
callouts.description: Energy asks a building to rely only on current solar income, meaning renewable energy (ILFI). Chapter 19 gives the order of work: cut the load first, then supply the rest from rooftop solar. Net zero is an annual balance, so the building still draws from the grid on some nights and exports in summer.

callouts.label: Net Positive Building
callouts.hint: Find the green building in the lower-right panel with a garden roof and solar panels, small arrows going in, and larger arrows of light, clean drops, and butterflies going out.
callouts.description: ILFI contrasts regeneration and net-positive outcomes with simply reducing harm. A net-positive building gives back more than it takes: surplus clean power, cleaner water leaving the site, and a richer habitat. The poster is a contrast of aims. Real projects still have to prove their results with measured performance.
